title: E‑commerce video ads in 2027: formats, specs and how to make them
summary: Make e‑commerce video ads that sell: formats and specs for Reels, TikTok, Shorts and Amazon, what works by product category, and how to produce them from photos.
body_markdown:
**You have a product people would love and photos that show it well** . But on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube Shorts, you're competing in feeds built for motion, where a still photo is easy to scroll past. **That's where e‑commerce video ads come in.**


The hard part isn’t knowing you need video. It’s producing it. A shoot means a studio, a crew and an edit. An agency costs more than most testing budgets allow. Creators take weeks. And **each platform expects something slightly different** : most e‑commerce video ads run vertically, in 9:16, on Reels, Stories, TikTok and YouTube Shorts, and in 4:5 or square in the Facebook and Instagram Feed, ideally between 6 and 30 seconds. Then you need a few versions of each to test.


The good news is that **if you already have product photos, you don't need a shoot to get there** .[Photoroom's Video Ad Maker](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/video-generator/ad-maker) turns your product images into short video ads: it plans the shots, drafts the script and voiceover, and exports each ad ready for the platform it will run on. Because every ad starts from photos of your real product, it shows customers exactly what they'll receive.


This guide goes deeper into each of these: the specs for every placement, how to structure an ad that sells, the four ways to produce one, and what works for each product category. We’ll also show how to plan a full campaign across every placement from a single set of product photos using Photoroom.


## **What are e‑commerce video ads?**


E‑commerce video ads are short paid videos that promote a product an online store sells, shown in placements like Instagram Reels, TikTok's For You feed, YouTube Shorts or Amazon search results. Their job is to stop the scroll, show the product clearly, and send the viewer to a product page to buy.


They differ from other video advertising in one important way: the product itself is the message. A brand film can sell a feeling. An e‑commerce ad has to show the real item[accurately](https://www.photoroom.com/glossary/fidelity) , because the viewer can buy it a few seconds later and will expect the same thing to arrive at their door.


## **Product video vs video ad: what's the difference?**


A product video helps someone who is already interested decide to buy. **A video ad has to win attention from someone who wasn't looking for you.** That difference changes almost every production choice.

Where it plays Product page, marketplace listings Feeds, Stories, search results, between other content

Volume is the biggest difference. A[product page](https://www.photoroom.com/glossary/product-page) can live with one great video for months. A paid campaign burns through creative. Ads that run to the same audience for weeks lose their effect, so **you need new versions regularly, and every version needs to be in the right specs for each placement.**


## **Which video ad formats should e‑commerce brands make?**


Use 9:16 vertical for Instagram and Facebook Reels and Stories, TikTok and YouTube Shorts. Use 4:5 or 1:1 for the Facebook and Instagram Feed and for Pinterest. Use 16:9 horizontal for Amazon Sponsored Brands video and Walmart Sponsored Videos. Most product ads work best at 6 to 30 seconds, with the product on screen in the first second.


Here’s what each placement asks for, and what tends to work for products.


### **Instagram and Facebook Reels ads**


Reels ads play full screen between organic Reels, usually with sound on. They look and feel like native content, so polished studio footage can stand out in the wrong way. A fast product reveal, a quick demo or a UGC-style clip works better.


### **Instagram and Facebook Stories ads**


Stories ads appear between friends’ Stories, and people tap through them fast. They suit short, direct messages: a launch teaser, a limited-time offer, or a “new colors are here” announcement. Stick to one idea per ad, with a clear call to action before the viewer taps away.


### **Facebook and Instagram Feed video ads**


Feed ads play in the main scrolling feed, in a 4:5 or square frame. Motion is the hook here: a product spinning, a before and after, or the product in use.


### **TikTok in-feed ads**


TikTok in-feed ads play full screen in the For You feed, with sound. Ads that feel like TikTok content do better than ads that feel like TV spots, so UGC-style videos, trend formats and hands-on demos are the natural fit.


### **YouTube Shorts ads**


Shorts ads play in the Shorts feed between vertical videos. Google recommends 10 to 30 seconds for ads that drive action, and advises adding sound such as music or voiceover. Product demos and the product in motion work well.


### **Pinterest video ads**


Pinterest video ads appear alongside the Pins people browse while they plan what to buy. That makes them a good fit for home, fashion, beauty and food brands. 6 to 15 seconds is the recommended length. People come to Pinterest for ideas, so show the product styled in a real setting rather than a hard sell.


### **Amazon and Walmart search video ads**


Amazon Sponsored Brands video and Walmart Sponsored Videos both appear in search results, next to the products a shopper is comparing. The viewer already wants to buy something in your category, so your video should explain why yours is the right choice. Focus on one or two benefits and make every claim readable on screen. Walmart also advises getting the core message across within five seconds and ending on a branded end card, since its videos loop.

What these specs mean when you're creating the ads for your online store?:


-


**Plan for two masters.** One 9:16 and one 16:9 version of each ad covers Reels, Stories, TikTok, Shorts, Amazon and Walmart. Add a 4:5 or square cut for Feed and Pinterest.


-


**Show the product first.** Get it on screen in the first second. Viewers scroll past anything that takes longer.


-


**Design for sound off.** Amazon and Walmart videos autoplay muted, and many people scroll feeds without sound. The main benefit should be clear from the visuals and on-screen text alone.


-


**Mind the safe zones.** On vertical placements, the platform’s own buttons and captions cover the top and bottom of the frame. A price or logo placed at the bottom edge may be hidden.


-


**Don’t letterbox.** Putting a horizontal video inside a vertical frame with black or blurred bars wastes space, and Amazon and Walmart reject it.


-


**Check AI labels.** If your ads use AI-generated or AI-edited assets, check each platform’s labeling rules before you publish.


## **How to create e‑commerce video ads: in-house, agency, creators or AI**


There are four ways to produce video ads. None is best for every brand. The right route depends on how many ads you need, how often, and what you're starting from.


### **In-house production**


You shoot and edit the ads yourself or with your own team. You need a camera or a good phone, lighting, a clean set and someone who can edit. The upside is control: you can reshoot whenever you like, and the footage stays yours. The downside is time and cost. Each new size, hook or language means more editing, and production competes with everything else on your to-do list. In-house works best for brands that already have a creative team and a steady product pipeline.


### **Agency or freelance production**


A production agency or freelance videographer handles the concept, shoot and edit. You get a polished result and expertise in storytelling, lighting and pacing. In exchange, you'll write a brief, wait through review rounds, and pay a budget that makes sense for a few hero videos, not dozens of test variations. This route suits brand campaigns, TV-style spots and launches where one standout video matters more than volume.


### **UGC creators**


You send products to creators, who film themselves using or talking about them. What you get goes beyond the video itself: your brand appears through a real person with their own audience, voice and credibility. That presence builds awareness and trust in a way that's hard to recreate, and the ads feel native on TikTok and Reels. The trade-offs are time and predictability: results vary from one creator to the next, turnaround takes weeks once shipping is included, and you need to agree usage rights for paid ads upfront. UGC creators are the right choice for brands that want to grow their visibility through creators' audiences and build credibility, especially social-first brands with products that are easy to demo on camera.


### **AI video ads from product photos**


AI video ad makers don't all work the same way. Some generate footage from a text prompt, some build the ad around an AI avatar, and some assemble it from templates. For e‑commerce, the best case is a tool that starts from the product photos you already have, like[Photoroom’s Video Ad Maker](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/video-generator/ad-maker) , so the ad shows your real product rather than an AI-generated version of it. The strongest of these also plan the shots, draft the script and voiceover, and generate the video, so there’s no shoot to book, no samples to ship and no edit to wait for. For sellers without a production team or a big budget, or who need to produce at scale, test and iterate, that changes three things:


-


**Time:** your first ad takes minutes, not days or weeks, and each new version is made in the same session.


-


**Cost:** there's no studio, crew or creator fee for every new version, so each extra ad costs very little to produce.


-


**Testing:** because new versions are quick and cheap, you can try different hooks, styles and offers, and keep what works.


The output depends on what you put in: clean, well-lit product photos give the best results, so it's worth tidying them up before you start.

## **How to make AI video ads from product photos with Photoroom**


You can make a video ad in Photoroom in four steps, starting from the[product photos](https://www.photoroom.com/ai-product-photography) you already have.


### **Step 1: Add your product photos**


Open the[Video Ad Maker](https://app.photoroom.com/video-ad-maker) , upload one or more photos of the product, or pick images already in your Photoroom account, such as product shots you've edited before. Different angles give the AI more to work with: if we use our serum as an example, it means a front view, the back label, a close-up of the dropper and a texture shot. Clean, well-lit photos give the most accurate results, and you can[remove the background](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/background-remover) or fix the lighting in Photoroom first.


### **Step 2: Let Photoroom plan the ad**


You can specify your requests or let the Video Ad Maker guiding you into creating the ad. It suggests a video type, style and length for your goal, then drafts a shot-by-shot plan, a script and a voiceover. For the serum, the plan might be the dropper releasing a drop, the texture on skin, the bottle on a bathroom shelf, and an end card with your offer.


### **Step 3: Refine it before you generate**


Change anything that doesn't fit your brand: rewrite a line of the script, swap a shot, pick another voice or actor, change the language, or ask for a different tone in the chat. Because you approve the plan first, you don't spend credits on a video with the wrong message.


### **Step 4: Pick the format and generate**


Choose 9:16 for Reels, Stories, TikTok and YouTube Shorts, or 16:9 for Amazon and product pages, and a length of 5, 8 or 10 seconds. Generate and download the MP4. Before you upload it to your ad platform, check that the product's colors, shape and logo match the real item.
